task: This is a synthetic newspaper-writing exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes. Write from the reporting snapshot as of September 8, 2026. Write a headline and a 450–650-word AP-style reported feature about Relay Yard's reclaimed-building-material business and the paperwork and timing that stand between a salvaged item and its next use.

facts.text: A July 2026 yard note records Relay Yard employee Neri Havell matching a reclaimed door's tag to its dimensions and removal record before a builder's collection.
Relay Yard buys or receives materials from authorized building strip-outs and sells reusable stock to builders and household customers.
Its latest intake ledger tracks 160 accepted doors: 90 sold, 30 reserved and 40 still available.
A reservation is not a completed sale, and reserved stock can return to availability if the order is canceled.
The yard's standard reservation period is 14 days, after which storage arrangements must be agreed separately.
A common interior door is listed at $40, compared with one local supplier's $140 new-door quote of a similar size.
Condition, hardware, refinishing and fitting costs differ, so those sticker prices do not establish a universal installed saving.
The yard records known dimensions and origins but does not certify every salvaged product for structural or fire-rated use.
Architect Cera Mossen says specified performance records can be necessary before her clients can use an item for a particular purpose.
Mossen said, "A beam can look sound in the yard and still need evidence before it belongs in the design."
Unidentified coatings and missing test records can limit where materials are offered; the packet supplies no chemical test results for those items.
Owner Tavin Lorne says arriving materials and outgoing construction schedules rarely match exactly.
Lorne said, "The bargain has to wait somewhere between the building coming down and the next one being ready."
The business employs four people, including one who spends most working hours measuring, photographing and listing stock.
The yard pays for storage and handling even when donated material has no purchase price.
A demolition contractor has offered another batch of doors, but the yard has not accepted it because covered storage is nearly full.
The business has not released a net-profit figure or a verified carbon-saving total for its stock.
A reused component's suitability is assessed for the proposed use rather than inferred solely from its age or appearance.
Relay Yard occupies a former seed warehouse, with different aisles for measured items and stock still awaiting inspection.
The owner has no signed agreement to expand into the neighboring building.
